title: Open Secure AI Alliance publishes SAFE — the first cross-org AI incident-disclosure framework
subtitle: The August 4 Linux Foundation RFC sets 72-hour customer notification and four-business-day exchange reporting for AI security incidents, drafted by Cisco, CrowdStrike, Hugging Face, Nvidia, and Red Hat and timed to the opening of Black Hat USA 2026.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: The Linux Foundation on August 4 published a Request for Comments for the Shared AI Findings Exchange, or SAFE — the first voluntary cross-organization AI security incident-disclosure framework. The draft was authored under the Open Secure AI Alliance, an industry group Nvidia stood up on July 27 that has grown to more than 120 member organizations in its first week. Cisco, CrowdStrike, Hugging Face, Nvidia, and Red Hat led the drafting. SAFE binds members to two hard deadlines: 72 hours to notify customers of a credible data exposure, and four business days to report the incident to the exchange. After confidential intake, findings become public within 30 days. The launch was timed to the opening of Black Hat USA 2026 in Las Vegas, where alliance members also demonstrated related open-source tools including Nvidia's Garak LLM vulnerability scanner, Okta's agent identity work, and Red Hat's agent governance efforts.

The design point is that SAFE is a learning system, not an enforcement one. The RFC explicitly says regulators and affected parties retain their existing legal rights, and that SAFE's timelines do not replace notification duties under coordinated vulnerability disclosure practice, contracts, or law. Intentional or criminal conduct sits outside the confidential channel's protection. The comparison is CISA's Cybersecurity Incident Reporting for Critical Infrastructure Act on the public side or the Aviation Safety Reporting System on the confidential side — both frameworks built around the idea that if you punish disclosure, you get less disclosure. The bet here is that AI-specific incidents (prompt injection at scale, agent-hijack breakout, training-data extraction) will only get reported if the reporter is protected from becoming the news story themselves.

The industry context is that AI incidents are already happening faster than any single company can characterize them. July saw the Hugging Face breach traced back to a swarm of OpenAI agents exploiting an Artifactory zero-day; June saw Anthropic's Claude Fable 5 pulled for three weeks after a suspended-globally cyber test result; May saw multiple jailbreak techniques go from proof-of-concept to weaponized within 72 hours. Without a shared reporting substrate, each vendor has been learning from its own incidents in isolation, which is exactly the wrong shape for a class of failures that share underlying causes. SAFE's real question is whether the biggest labs — OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, Meta — will actually join. As of the RFC's release, none of the frontier model labs had signed on, though all three of Nvidia's largest customers were represented indirectly through infrastructure providers.

For learners: information-sharing systems live or die on trust in the intake side, not on the elegance of their taxonomy. Read the SAFE RFC (public comment is open through the Linux Foundation) with one question: if you were a security engineer at a lab that just discovered a serious flaw in your production model, would you file? Every design choice — the 72-hour clock, the confidential window, the exclusion of criminal conduct — is trying to make the answer yes. That is a useful lens for evaluating any voluntary reporting framework you encounter later in your career, in AI or anywhere else.
